old: Not every verb ending in る is a る-verb. Several end in -aru/-uru/-oru and are う-verbs (ある, 分かる, 帰る, 走る, the last a 'disguised' exception). old: Pegadinha de ordem das palavras: advérbios de frequência como いつも vão ANTES do verbo, nunca no fim da frase como às vezes fazemos em português ("eu vou sempre"). new: Pegadinha de ordem das palavras: advérbios de frequência como いつも vão ANTES do verbo, nunca no fim da frase como às vezes fazemos em português ("eu vou sempre"). Sozinho, いつも é sempre positivo ("sempre"). O sentido de "nunca" só aparece quando o VERBO está no negativo: いつも来ない ("nunca vem"). Em português temos um advérbio próprio para isso ("nunca"); em japonês quem nega é o verbo, e いつも só marca a frequência. Para frequências menores, compare com よく ("frequentemente"), ときどき ("às vezes"), たまに ("raramente").

The contrast with Portuguese was also drawn backwards, since pt-BR is the language that has a dedicated negative adverb. The record's own formation already states the rule correctly.

old: Word-order trap: frequency adverbs like いつも go BEFORE the verb, never at the end of the sentence as we sometimes do in Portuguese ('eu vou sempre'). Unlike Portuguese, いつも doesn't need negation to mean 'never': that sense comes from the verb being negative; on its own, いつも is positive. For lower frequencies, compare よく ('often'), ときどき ('sometimes'), たまに ('rarely').
new: Word-order trap: frequency adverbs like いつも go BEFORE the verb, never at the end of the sentence as we sometimes do in Portuguese ('eu vou sempre'). On its own, いつも is always positive ('always'). The 'never' sense only appears when the VERB is negative: いつも来ない ('never comes'). Portuguese has a dedicated adverb for that ('nunca'); in Japanese it is the verb that negates, and いつも only marks frequency. For lower frequencies, compare よく ('often'), ときどき ('sometimes'), たまに ('rarely').

Be careful too not to confuse this with na-adjectives, which conjugate differently.

old: It is a pattern that This is the CONTRAST pattern: you mention two elements and set one against the other. The structure is "[X]は … が、[Y]は …", where each は highlights (topicalizes) one element and が joins the two halves with the meaning "but"; it is not the subject が. E.g.: 日本語は話せますが、中国語は話せません (にほんごははなせますが、ちゅうごくごははなせません) = "Japanese I can speak, Chinese I can't"; コーヒーは飲みますが、お茶は飲みません = "coffee I drink, tea I don't." This contrastive は can take the place of the を or the が of the element being highlighted. Careful not to confuse this が with the sub-subject が of 象は鼻が長い (ぞうははながながい) = "the elephant has a long trunk," which is a different structure. to talk about ONE theme and, within it, contrast two things. The typical structure is 'Topic は A が [quality], B は [opposite quality].' Classic example: 象は鼻が長い (ぞうははながながい) = 'The elephant has a long trunk,' where は marks the general theme (elephant) and が marks the sub-subject (the trunk). When a second は appears, it usually creates contrast: 日本語は話せますが、中国語は話せません (にほんごははなせますが、ちゅうごくごははなせません) = 'Japanese I can speak, Chinese I can't.'.
